title: China sends 100-plus ships around Taiwan without announcing an exercise, Taipei says
dek: Taiwan says more than 100 Chinese navy and coast guard vessels are spread across the western Pacific, with two aircraft carriers at sea. Beijing has announced no exercise, less than two weeks before Xi Jinping hosts Donald Trump at APEC.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
China has spread more than 100 navy and coast guard vessels across the western Pacific around Taiwan in what US analysts describe as possibly the largest unannounced Chinese military exercise of recent years, rehearsing how Beijing might surround and cut off the island. Beijing has not announced any exercise, and its foreign ministry has not addressed the deployment directly.

Taiwan's National Security Council secretary-general, Joseph Wu, raised the alarm on Tuesday, writing on X that China had "100+ vessels in the #WesternPacific as of now" and calling Beijing a "big bully". "We won't provoke, but we won't bow to any pressure," he wrote. Two of China's three aircraft carriers are at sea. The deployment comes less than two weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to host US President Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November.

## What happened

According to Mr Wu's figures, as summarised by researchers at the American Enterprise Institute (AEI) and the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), the ships are grouped in two main concentrations: four task forces drawn from three of the People's Liberation Army's five theatre commands, operating in the open ocean between Taiwan and the US territory of Guam, and a closer ring of at least six China Coast Guard vessels and other naval ships around Taiwan itself. The figures do not say how many of the 100-plus vessels are warships and how many are coast guard ships.

The carrier Liaoning and its escorts entered the western Pacific through the Basilan Strait in the southern Philippines between 23 and 26 October, the AEI-ISW update said, and are operating between Taiwan and Guam. Satellite images from 2 November showed the newer carrier Fujian leaving its base at Sanya on Hainan island and heading east, possibly towards southern Taiwan. At least three other major warships left Sanya between 26 October and 2 November. In all, the analysts said, the deployment includes two carriers and at least four of China's ten guided-missile cruisers.

Activity in the air has risen too. Taiwan's defence ministry said it tracked 49 Chinese military aircraft sorties in the 24 hours to 6 am on Tuesday, 31 of which crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait, along with six navy and six other official Chinese ships. In the following 24 hours it counted 22 aircraft and seven naval vessels, and said it had tracked 90 aircraft and 37 ships around the island so far in November.

The coast guard has been busy closer to shore. Early on Saturday, 31 October, a Chinese coast guard vessel came within about one nautical mile of a Taiwanese coast guard ship near the Taiwan-held Pratas Islands in the South China Sea, more than 400 km south-west of Taiwan, before being asked to leave. Taiwan's coast guard said it was the 13th such intrusion near Pratas this year, involving 16 vessels, and called on Beijing "to immediately cease these pointless acts of harassment". The same day, two Chinese coast guard ships patrolled east of Taiwan and challenged passing shipping by radio, Taiwan said. China's coast guard called it a routine law-enforcement patrol in waters under its jurisdiction and said it would intensify such patrols. Taiwan's coast guard replied that China "has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan's waters."

## How it differs from earlier drills

China has staged several large named exercises around Taiwan in recent years, most recently "Justice Mission 2025", announcing them as warnings to what it calls separatist forces. This time it has announced nothing. The AEI-ISW analysts assessed that the deployment may be a "major, unannounced military exercise simulating surrounding and isolating Taiwan", larger than Justice Mission 2025, and said the decision not to announce it "departs from recent precedent". They suggested the silence may be meant to show that the PLA can isolate Taiwan at will, and to erode Taiwanese confidence in its own defence and in US willingness to help. China has not described the purpose of the ships' movements. When the Liaoning first sailed for western Pacific training in mid-October, China's navy said the deployment was not aimed at any country or target.

## Background

Beijing claims Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out force to take it; Taiwan's elected government rejects the claim. China's pressure has grown through 2026. Its coast guard now patrols regularly east of Taiwan, waters it did not routinely enter before, and Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement in June about Chinese activity there. Earlier this week, analysts reported that Chinese research ships had lingered over undersea cables near Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines.

China's quarrel with Japan over Taiwan is also unresolved. At a regular briefing in Beijing on Friday, marking a year since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said a Taiwan emergency could involve Japan's armed forces, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the "current serious difficulties in China-Japan relations are entirely the responsibility of the Japanese side" and that "the pressing priority is to correct the erroneous words and deeds on the Taiwan question". He was not asked about the naval deployment.

## Reactions

Kuan Bi-ling, head of Taiwan's Ocean Affairs Council, which oversees the coast guard, told a sea-drone forum in Tainan on Monday: "Taiwan's ocean must be surveyed by ourselves, and we must master our own information." Neither Washington nor Tokyo had made a public statement on the deployment by Saturday, as far as could be established.

## Why it matters for India

India is not a party to the Taiwan dispute and does not recognise Taiwan as a state, but it has a direct stake in the waters around it. A large share of India's trade with Japan, South Korea, China and the Pacific coast of the Americas passes through the South China Sea and the seas east of Taiwan, and any blockade or exclusion zone would push up freight and insurance costs, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has done this year for Gulf oil. Taiwan is also the world's main maker of advanced semiconductors; India's electronics and car industries, and its own new chip plants, depend on supplies that a crisis around the island would disrupt.

The deployment also overlaps with the US-led Malabar naval exercise off Japan, in which the Indian frigate INS Sahyadri joined US, Japanese and Australian ships this week. China's ability to put two carrier groups and more than 100 vessels to sea at once also says something about a navy that is expanding its reach into the Indian Ocean.

## What happens next

The immediate test is whether the ships stay at sea into the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, where Mr Xi is expected to meet Mr Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung. Taiwan holds local elections on 28 November, and President Lai Ching-te has warned of more disinformation and cyber attacks before the vote. Taiwan's defence ministry publishes daily counts of Chinese aircraft and ships around the island, which will show whether the deployment is winding down.

## Key numbers

- 100+: Chinese navy and coast guard vessels in the western Pacific, according to Taiwan's National Security Council (3 November)
- 2: Chinese aircraft carriers at sea, the Liaoning and the Fujian
- 49: Chinese military aircraft sorties around Taiwan in the 24 hours to 6 am on 3 November, according to Taiwan's defence ministry
- 18-19 November: APEC summit in Shenzhen
